title: Essay titles for revision
description: Two more essay titles from this week’s lectures. Note them down for revision, and write either of them here for practice.
instructions:
Optional, for revision. These are more essay titles that go with this week’s lectures. It’s worth noting them down, as they’re good practice for the exam. Only the Supervision 5 essay needs to be handed in.

  • You can write either of them here for practice, as you would in the exam: about 40 minutes each, without notes.
  • Planning an answer to each one (your argument, your evidence and the order you’d put them in) is good revision too. Note which equation each point uses.
  • After you submit, Review my answers shows you the ground each title covers.

questions.title: The heart and the cardiac output
questions.text: “The heart is necessary for cardiac output, but it does not normally limit it.” Discuss.
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer. Dr Fraser suggests the venous return equation, CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR, as the plan.

  • The evidence for the quotation. Guyton replaced the right heart of dogs with a pump: below normal, less pumping reduced the cardiac output (the heart is necessary), but more pumping didn’t raise it (it doesn’t normally limit it).
  • Why: the circulation is a closed system. Like a pump inside a balloon, the heart can move blood from the veins to the arteries, but it can’t change the mean pressure of the system, the mean systemic filling pressure (MSFP). Flow = (PA − PV) / R, and the heart can’t widen the pressure difference beyond the point where the veins collapse, 1 or 2 mmHg below zero. A healthy heart already holds RAP close to zero, even at rest.
  • What sets MSFP. Only about the last 20% of the blood volume (the stressed volume) stretches the vessel walls, giving an MSFP of 7–10 mmHg. So, without venoconstriction, losing 10% of the blood roughly halves MSFP, and a 20% rise in volume doubles it. The veins are about ten times as compliant as the arteries and hold most of the blood, so venoconstriction raises MSFP (keeping it above zero until about 40% of the blood is lost), while constricting the arterioles raises TPR but not MSFP.
  • More evidence. Pacing the heart faster doesn’t raise the cardiac output unless venous return rises, but an arteriovenous fistula shows that the heart can pump much more when more blood returns. The cardiac output follows MSFP, raised by filling the circulation or by venoconstriction, and not the heart rate.
  • The heart’s part. By Starling’s law the heart pumps what returns to it, keeping RAP close to zero, so a higher MSFP gives a higher cardiac output. A higher afterload makes it contract more strongly, so a higher TPR raises ABP rather than lowering the cardiac output (the microsphere experiments). The autonomic nerves change its rate and contractility, which matters when MSFP rises too, as in exercise. Guyton’s curves put this together: the cardiac output is where the venous return and cardiac function curves cross.
  • “Normally”: when the heart does limit it. In heart failure the cardiac function curve falls, so the output falls and RAP rises. Fluid retention and venoconstriction raise MSFP, which restores the output only partly, at the cost of a still higher atrial pressure and oedema. In exercise, too, the heart must be stimulated if the higher venous return is to be pumped without RAP rising.
  • Evaluate. RvR isn’t the resistance of any one set of vessels. It lumps together everything that hinders the return of blood to the heart. And Guyton’s curves are a model. In exercise it may be better to think of the muscle pump and the heart as two pumps in series.

questions.title: Arterial blood pressure and its control in exercise
questions.text: Why is arterial blood pressure the principal controlled variable of the circulation? How is it regulated in exercise?
questions.guidance:
Here are some points to consider. It isn’t a model answer. Dr Fraser suggests ABP = CO × TPR, with CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR, as the plan: for any challenge, ask what it does to TPR and to MSFP, how the change is detected or predicted, and which effectors keep ABP up.

  • Why ABP. With the mean arterial pressure held constant, each tissue can set its own flow just by changing the resistance of its arterioles: a constant-pressure, variable-flow system. The cardiac output isn’t measured anywhere in the body. It’s regulated to hold ABP. And the mean stays nearly constant when the pulse pressure changes (with a leaking aortic valve, or in exercise, where it rises only a little), which suggests that the mean is what’s regulated.
  • Two handles. ABP = CO × TPR, and because the afterload has little effect on the cardiac output, CO and TPR can be controlled largely independently.
  • Sensors. High-pressure baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch, shown by Heymans’ cross-circulation experiments. They’re most sensitive near the normal mean pressure, and they reset if it changes for long. Without them ABP becomes far more variable, but its mean is unchanged, so they serve short-term control. Arterial chemoreceptors join in when ABP is below about 60 mmHg. Low-pressure receptors in the atria and great veins report filling, and act on the blood volume through ADH, renal sympathetic activity and thirst. With both kinds of baroreceptor denervated, the mean rises.
  • Integration and effectors. The medulla (nucleus tractus solitarius, vasomotor and cardioinhibitory areas) drives sympathetic constriction of arterioles (TPR) and veins (MSFP), sympathetic stimulation of the heart (β1), adrenaline from the adrenal medulla, and the tonically active vagus to the heart.
  • Exercise: the challenge. TPR may fall to about 20% of its resting value, so to hold ABP the cardiac output must rise about five-fold. Venous return rises as venoconstriction raises MSFP two- to three-fold and the muscle pump halves RvR, while the heart’s rate and contractility rise so that RAP stays close to zero.
  • Exercise: the control. Feedforward, because feedback would need ABP to fall first: central command from the cortex and cerebellum, and signals from muscle and joint receptors (the heart rate rises before exercise begins, and in the curare experiment an attempted handgrip raises it as much as a real one). The baroreflex is reset to a higher set point, so ABP rises a little, mostly as a higher systolic pressure.
  • Evaluate. This is short-term control. Over longer periods the blood volume, regulated by the kidney, sets MSFP and so ABP. The same responses can do harm, as in heart failure.
